name: Dark
lede: Dark is a near-black blue, recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary as first used in 1915, later folded into one ISCC-NBS 1955 block under several other names.

sections.title: A dictionary word, not a description
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* first records this name in 1915, on plate 6, position L 8 [1]. The ISCC-NBS 1955 dictionary lists the same block under three separate names, Mascot Blackish, Semi-Gloss, and Transatlantic Blue, all pointing at the same small, blackish-blue region [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[black-blue]], [[midnight-navy]], [[midnight-navy]] and [[bagdad]], at 3.7, 4.1, 4.1 and 4.9 ΔE [1]. It has no Munsell notation on file, and the nearest family colors are [[black]], [[dark-green|Dark Green]], [[navy]], and [[charcoal]], all occupying the same low-lightness end of the wheel [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this near-black in 482 of 23,781 paintings, about 2 percent, as photographed [2]. It sits almost entirely in the shadows: 95 percent of its appearances rank as the darkest tone in their painting's six-color palette [2]. [[painter:johannes-vermeer|Vermeer]] carries it nearly seven times the archive's average rate, and the earliest dated hit is a 1325 altarpiece by Ugolino di Nerio, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It covers the most canvas in John Neagle's 1836 *Thomas W. Dyott*, a near-black coat against a near-black ground [2]. These are computed color matches on aged, varnished photographs, not pigment identifications [2].
